title: Episode 88: Caesar Rodney's Midnight Ride: The Gallop That Saved Independence
description:
Caesar Rodney's Midnight Ride: The Gallop That Saved Independence. How an ailing Delaware delegate rode eighty grueling miles on horseback through a torrential thunderstorm to cast the decisive vote for the Declaration of Independence on July 2, 1776. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into the American Revolution.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. On the humid afternoon of July 1, 1776, inside the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia, the Continental Congress stood on the precipice of American independence. Virginia delegate Richard Henry Lee's resolution declaring the colonies free and independent states was brought to a preliminary vote. Nine colonies voted yes. But Delaware—a critical middle colony—was hopelessly deadlocked: delegate Thomas McKean voted yes, while delegate George Read voted no. Without Delaware, the fragile unity of the thirteen colonies would shatter. Knowing that Caesar Rodney, the third Delaware delegate, was eighty miles away at his farm in Dover, McKean dispatched an urgent courier into the night. Battling facial cancer, asthma, and a raging summer thunderstorm, Caesar Rodney mounted his horse and rode through the dark to change the course of history. George brings us the heroic story of Caesar Rodney's midnight ride.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MAN FROM DOVER GREEN
In the turbulent summer of seventeen seventy-six, Caesar Rodney was one of the most respected, experienced, and dedicated public servants in the American colonies. Born in seventeen twenty-eight on a sprawling eight-hundred-acre plantation called Byfield near Dover, Delaware, Rodney had dedicated his life to civic leadership, serving as high sheriff of Kent County, speaker of the Delaware colonial assembly, associate justice of the supreme court, and brigadier general of the Delaware militia. But Rodney's tireless public service came at an immense physical cost. For years, Rodney had suffered from a severe, disfiguring facial cancer that eroded the flesh of his left cheek and jaw. To spare friends and constituents from the gruesome sight, Rodney wore a green silk scarf or leather veil tied around his face. He also suffered from chronic asthma and painful gout that made physical travel excruciating. Yet despite constant physical agony, Rodney possessed a buoyant spirit, razor-sharp wit, and an unshakeable commitment to American liberty that commanded the deep respect of fellow patriots like George Washington and John Adams. Rodney was an admired political leader whose dry wit, courteous demeanor, and deep integrity made him a unifying figure among Delaware contentious political factions during the turbulent countdown to revolution. Despite the agonizing pain of his facial cancer, Rodney refused to withdraw from public life, wearing a green silk veil to conceal his disfigurement while presiding over the Delaware colonial assembly with dignity. As speaker of the Delaware Assembly and brigadier general of militia, Rodney possessed rare moral authority throughout the Lower Counties.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DEADLOCK IN PHILADELPHIA
In late June seventeen seventy-six, the Continental Congress in Philadelphia was debating the momentous question of total separation from the British Empire. Under the rules of the Congress, each colony cast a single vote determined by the majority of its attending delegates. Furthermore, John Adams and the independence faction recognized that unanimity was essential: if a single colony voted against independence, King George the Third and European allies would see the rebellion as divided and doomed. On Monday, July first, a preliminary vote was taken on the floor of the Pennsylvania State House. Pennsylvania and South Carolina voted no; New York abstained pending instructions; and Delaware was tied. Thomas McKean, a passionate Scotch-Irish Presbyterian lawyer, voted enthusiastically for independence. But George Read, a conservative Delaware attorney who believed reconciliation was still possible and that the colonies were not yet militarily prepared for total war, voted firmly against. Delaware's third delegate, Caesar Rodney, was absent, eighty miles south in Dover, where he had been managing Delaware militia regiments to suppress Loyalist uprisings. The debate inside the Pennsylvania State House was tense and historic, with John Adams delivering passionate arguments for immediate separation while George Read cautioned that premature independence would bring military ruin. The delegates in Philadelphia knew that European powers, particularly France and Spain, would never offer military alliances or financial loans to a divided rebellion whose middle colonies hesitated to declare total independence. With Thomas McKean voting for independence and George Read voting against, Delaware's critical delegation was hopelessly deadlocked.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE URGENT COURIER INTO THE NIGHT
Recognizing that the final, binding vote was scheduled for the morning of Tuesday, July second, Thomas McKean refused to let the cause of independence fail. Stepping into the hallway, McKean hired an express courier at his own expense, handing him an urgent dispatch addressed to General Caesar Rodney in Dover. The message was brief and stark: Delaware was deadlocked; the fate of the American republic hung in the balance; Rodney must come to Philadelphia immediately. The courier spurred his horse southward across the dusty post roads, galloping through the night and arriving at Rodney's farmhouse near Dover on the morning of July first. Rodney read the letter, looked at his weeping family who begged him not to undertake the dangerous journey in his frail condition, and did not hesitate for a single second. Donning his boots, his military spurs, and securing his green silk veil over his cancer-ravaged face, Rodney ordered his favorite horse saddled. By early afternoon on July first, Caesar Rodney rode out into the gathering storm. Thomas McKean express courier arrived at Rodney farm in Dover with lathered horses, delivering the urgent plea that without Rodney immediate arrival in Philadelphia, Delaware would vote against independence. Rodney kissed his family goodbye and mounted his horse on the Dover green, knowing that an eighty-mile ride through thunderstorm gales in his fragile condition could easily prove fatal to his weakened body. McKean's emergency courier spurred his horse southward across muddy roads, knowing Delaware's vote could tip the historic continental balance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: EIGHTY MILES THROUGH THE THUNDERSTORM
The eighty-mile journey from Dover to Philadelphia along the King's Highway was a grueling ordeal that tested the absolute limits of human endurance. As afternoon turned to evening, a violent summer thunderstorm swept over the Delaware Valley. Lightning split the black sky, deafening thunder shook the forest, and torrential sheets of tropical rain turned the unpaved dirt post road into a treacherous river of ankle-deep mud and flooded clay gullies. Rodney rode through the night, his horse's hooves splashing through flooded creeks and stumbling over hidden tree roots in the pitch dark. At regular post stages—in Smyrna, Cantwell's Bridge, and New Castle—Rodney paused only long enough to leap from his lathered, exhausted horse and mount a fresh steed, refusing food or rest. The cold rain soaked through his heavy wool riding coat, chilling his feverish body, while the damp air triggered severe asthma attacks that left him gasping for breath in the saddle. Yet driven by the burning flame of duty, Rodney rode on through the stormy darkness, mile after agonizing mile. Rodney spurred his horse through torrential summer thunderstorms, riding through swollen streams and ankle-deep clay roads while battling severe asthma attacks and the agonizing pain of facial cancer. At each post station, stable hands marveled at the veiled rider fierce determination, watching him change horses in minutes and gallop back into the stormy night without pausing for food or shelter. Through blinding flashes of lightning and howling winds, Rodney galloped without rest through the night, changing exhausted horses at relay posts.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ARRIVAL AT THE PENNSYLVANIA STATE HOUSE
On the morning of Tuesday, July second, seventeen seventy-six, the delegates to the Continental Congress assembled inside the Pennsylvania State House for the final, historic vote. Thomas McKean paced anxiously outside on the front steps, staring down Chestnut Street, checking his pocket watch as the minutes ticked away toward the opening gavel. The morning debate began, and John Hancock called the assembly to order. Inside the humid chamber, South Carolina had reversed its vote to yes, and Pennsylvania's conservative delegates had agreed to stay away, allowing Pennsylvania to vote yes. Just as the roll call for Delaware was about to be called, the sound of galloping hooves echoed across the cobblestones outside. A mud-splattered horse wheezed to a halt in front of the building. Thomas McKean cheered as Caesar Rodney, soaked to the skin, boots caked in thick mud, and riding whip still in his gloved hand, dismounted and walked stiffly up the stone steps, supported by McKean's arm. Thomas McKean paced the stone steps of the state house in Philadelphia under the morning sun, his anxiety mounting with every passing minute as the opening gavel of the final roll call approached. The Continental Congress was preparing to call the roll of the thirteen colonies when the sound of galloping hooves announced the arrival of the missing Delaware delegate outside on Chestnut Street. Soaked in mud and clutching his dripping cloak, the gaunt delegate strode into the state house just as the morning session commenced.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TIE-BREAKING VOTE FOR LIBERTY
At shortly after nine o'clock in the morning, Caesar Rodney entered the historic chamber, his arrival stunning the assembled delegates into silence. Without taking time to change out of his mud-stained riding clothes or remove his spurs, Rodney walked down the center aisle to the Delaware table, sitting beside George Read and Thomas McKean. When the secretary called the roll for the Colony of Delaware, Caesar Rodney rose to his feet. Standing tall despite his racking cough and disfigured face, Rodney addressed the Congress in a clear, resonant voice that rang across the room: 'As I believe the voice of my constituents and of all fair and sensible men is for independence; and my own judgment concurs with them, I vote for independence!' Delaware's vote was officially cast in the affirmative. The deadlock was broken. Twelve colonies voted for independence, with none opposing. The United States of America was born. Caesar Rodney arrival in mud-caked boots and riding spurs electrified the chamber, and his resounding vote for independence broke the Delaware deadlock, ensuring the unanimous birth of the American republic. Rodney resounding declaration that his voice was for independence ensured that the Lee Resolution passed without a single dissenting colony, establishing the United States as an independent nation on July second. John Adams recorded that Rodney arrived just in the nick of time, casting Delaware's decisive affirmative vote for American independence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PATRIOT'S ETERNAL RIDE
Caesar Rodney went on to sign the formal parchment Declaration of Independence on August second, seventeen seventy-six, and served as President of Delaware throughout the darkest years of the Revolutionary War, coordinating troop supplies and military defense for George Washington's army. In seventeen eighty-four, at the age of fifty-five, Rodney finally succumbed to the cancer he had fought for over a decade, buried in an unmarked grave on his beloved Byfield plantation. But his eighty-mile midnight gallop through the storm remains one of the most heroic and pivotal feats of the American founding. In nineteen ninety-nine, when the United States Mint launched the 50 State Quarters program, the very first quarter released honored Delaware, depicting Caesar Rodney galloping on horseback on his historic midnight ride. Today, on Dover Green and in the halls of the Delaware State Capitol, Caesar Rodney's courage reminds every generation of Americans that liberty is not won by passive consensus, but by the relentless devotion of ordinary patriots who will ride through the storm to do their duty. Rodney signed the parchment Declaration of Independence in August seventeen seventy-six, risking the gallows for high treason against King George III and cementing his name among the immortal founders of American liberty. Caesar Rodney midnight gallop remains one of the most iconic moments in American revolutionary history, honored on Delaware state quarter and celebrated as an eternal symbol of patriotic sacrifice. Caesar Rodney's courage and dedication ensured that Delaware would forever be celebrated as the First State of American liberty.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Caesar Rodney's midnight ride proved that one man's courage and a galloping horse could change the destiny of a nation. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey along the banks of the Brandywine River in Delaware for the explosive history of the DuPont Gunpowder Mills.
